rows.experiment_summary: This first experiment established a minimal baseline using RNA-only modality, a single profile, and a PCA(2000) encoder with no image input, aggregation, or fusion. The validation accuracy of 0.485 (F1: 0.464) provides an initial reference point for the raw RNA signal under this deterministic, untrained encoder setup, but with no prior experiments for comparison, the result cannot be attributed to any specific design choice. It serves as a performance floor from which the incremental contribution of multiprofile aggregation, alternative encoders, image modality, and fusion strategies can be assessed in subsequent experiments.
rows.selection_reason: With no prior experiments completed, there is zero evidence about which design axes (modality, encoder, profile, aggregation, fusion) matter most. The highest-priority uncertainty is establishing a clean performance floor. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the most minimal configuration in the search space: it uses a single modality (RNA), a single profile (no aggregation needed), and PCA (a deterministic, fast, well-understood encoder with no training variability). This isolates the raw RNA signal quality as a reference point. From this baseline, subsequent experiments can cleanly measure the incremental contribution of each design choice—adding multiprofile (config_002/003), swapping encoders (config_004/007), adding the image modality (config_016/022), or introducing aggregation and fusion—without confounding multiple variables. Choosing the simplest possible baseline first maximizes the interpretability of every future comparison and is the most information-efficient use of the first experiment under a limited budget.

rows.experiment_summary: This experiment tested whether the image modality alone, encoded by ResNet-50 with a single profile and no aggregation or fusion, carries discriminative signal, yielding a validation accuracy of ~0.208 (F1: ~0.172). This is substantially below the RNA-only PCA(2000) single-profile baseline of ~0.485 (F1: ~0.464), suggesting that in this configuration the image modality provides limited discriminative information, though the comparison is confounded by the fundamentally different encoder types (pretrained CNN vs. linear PCA) and cannot definitively attribute the gap to image content versus encoder choice. It remains uncertain whether alternative image encoders, preprocessing, or fusion with the stronger RNA signal could recover useful information from the image modality, leaving open whether the multimodal branch of the design space warrants further search budget.
rows.selection_reason: The only completed experiment (config_001) establishes that RNA-only with PCA and a single profile yields ~0.485 accuracy, giving us a reference for the RNA signal. The largest remaining uncertainty is whether the image modality carries any discriminative signal at all. If image contributes nothing, then all 36 multimodal configurations become low-priority, dramatically reshaping the search. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is a clean, single-variable test: it isolates the image signal using a standard, well-understood encoder (ResNet-50) while keeping the profile setting minimal. This is the highest-information next experiment because the answer (image helps vs. doesn't) determines whether the multimodal branch of the design space is worth further budget, and it avoids confounding the image effect with multiprofile aggregation or fusion choices.

rows.experiment_summary: This experiment tested multiprofile aggregation (avgpool) on the RNA-only PCA-2000 branch, changing only the profile setting from single to multi relative to llm_summary_001 while holding encoder, modality, and fusion fixed. The validation accuracy improved to ~0.591 (F1: ~0.573) from the single-profile baseline of ~0.485 (F1: ~0.464), indicating that multiprofile aggregation via avgpool yields a meaningful gain over the single-profile configuration under this encoder. It remains uncertain whether alternative aggregation strategies (e.g., maxpool, attention-weighted) could further improve performance, and whether this multiprofile advantage persists when the RNA branch is combined with image modality or fusion in downstream multimodal configurations.
rows.selection_reason: Evidence: Two experiments establish that RNA (PCA-2000, single profile) yields 0.485 accuracy while image (ResNet-50, single profile) yields only 0.208, confirming RNA as the dominant signal. However, we have no information on whether multiprofile aggregation can improve the RNA branch. Uncertainty: It is unknown whether aggregating multiple profiles (here via avgpool) with the same PCA-2000 encoder meaningfully improves over the single-profile baseline, and this axis (profile setting + aggregation) is orthogonal to encoder choice and will affect the design of all downstream multimodal configurations. This experiment (config_002) changes exactly one variable from config_001—profile_setting from single to multi with avgpool aggregation—while holding encoder, modality, and fusion fixed. This isolates the effect of multiprofile aggregation cleanly. It is the best use of the next budget slot because: (1) it directly extends the best-performing baseline, (2) a positive result validates the entire multiprofile branch (configs 003, 005-009, 018-027, etc.), while a null or negative result redirects search toward single-profile and encoder variation, and (3) it reduces uncertainty about a design axis that is shared across the majority of remaining configurations, making the result broadly informative for subsequent decisions.

rows.experiment_summary: This experiment tested transformer aggregation in place of avgpool on the RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000 branch, changing only the aggregation strategy relative to llm_summary_003 to isolate its effect. Validation accuracy dropped to ~0.519 (F1: ~0.480) from ~0.591 (F1: ~0.573) under avgpool, indicating that in this clean single-variable comparison, transformer aggregation underperformed simple averaging by approximately 0.07 in accuracy. It remains uncertain whether this gap generalizes to multimodal configurations where transformer aggregation might better handle heterogeneous feature distributions, or whether the observed underperformance reflects a limitation of the transformer architecture under the current data regime rather than a fundamental disadvantage of attention-based aggregation.
rows.selection_reason: Evidence: config_002 (RNA, multiprofile, PCA-2000, avgpool) achieved 0.591 accuracy, a +0.106 gain over the single-profile baseline (config_001, 0.485), confirming that multiprofile aggregation is a major performance driver. However, we have only tested one aggregation strategy (avgpool) and do not yet know whether the aggregation mechanism itself matters or whether avgpool is simply 'good enough.' Question: config_003 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding modality (RNA), profile setting (multiprofile), and encoder (PCA-2000) fixed relative to config_002, giving a clean single-variable comparison that isolates the effect of aggregation strategy. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It is the cleanest possible 1-factor comparison in the current design space, avoiding confounds from encoder or modality changes. (2) The aggregation choice is a critical design axis that will directly affect all downstream multimodal configurations—knowing whether transformer aggregation adds value over simple averaging determines whether we should invest budget in transformer-based fusion later. (3) If transformer significantly outperforms avgpool, it reveals a high-value design lever; if it performs similarly or worse, it confirms avgpool is sufficient and redirects budget toward encoder or modality questions. (4) Under a limited budget, resolving this uncertainty early prevents committing multiple multimodal experiments to a suboptimal aggregation strategy.

rows.experiment_summary: This experiment tested a learned nonlinear RNA encoder (scvi_n200) in place of the linear PCA-2000 projection, holding modality (RNA-only), profile setting (multiprofile), and aggregation (avgpool) fixed relative to llm_summary_003 to isolate the encoder effect. Validation accuracy improved to ~0.650 (F1: ~0.628) from ~0.591 (F1: ~0.573) under PCA-2000, indicating in this clean single-variable comparison that the learned encoder captures structure beyond what the linear projection provides. It remains uncertain whether this encoder advantage generalizes to alternative aggregation strategies or persists when the RNA branch is combined with the image modality in multimodal fusion settings, and whether other learned encoders or latent dimensions could yield further gains.
rows.selection_reason: Evidence: The RNA branch dominates (0.591 with PCA-2000/multiprofile/avgpool vs 0.208 image-only), and multiprofile avgpool is the best aggregation. The key uncertainty is whether a learned nonlinear encoder (scvi_n200) can capture structure that linear PCA-2000 misses, since all RNA results so far use a deterministic linear projection. This experiment (config_005: RNA-only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_002, isolating the encoder effect while holding profile, aggregation, and modality fixed. It is the best use of the next budget slot because: (1) the RNA representation is the dominant performance driver, so clarifying whether a learned encoder helps is the highest-impact design question; (2) the answer directly determines which RNA encoder to carry into any future multimodal fusion experiments, preventing wasted budget on suboptimal encoder choices in more complex configurations; (3) it avoids the risk of prematurely investing in multimodal fusion when the image signal is very weak and the RNA branch may still have untapped headroom.

rows.experiment_summary: This experiment tested whether adding a ResNet50 image branch via concat fusion to the best-known RNA configuration (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) improves validation accuracy over the RNA-only baseline, yielding ~0.632 accuracy (F1: ~0.607) compared to ~0.650 (F1: ~0.628) for the RNA-only scvi_n200 setup (llm_summary_005). The slight degradation (~0.019 in accuracy) suggests that in this specific configuration the image branch did not provide a net benefit and may have introduced mild interference, though the small magnitude and the fact that only one fusion strategy (concat) and one image encoder (ResNet50) were tested mean this does not definitively rule out complementary image signal. It remains uncertain whether alternative fusion mechanisms (e.g., attention, gating) or stronger image encoders (e.g., ViT-L) could recover or exceed the RNA-only performance, leaving the broader multimodal design space partially open but currently unsupported by positive evidence.
rows.selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: The RNA branch is well-characterized (scvi_n200 + multiprofile + avgpool = 0.650 is the current best), but the image modality's contribution in a fused setting is completely untested. Image-only ResNet50 was very weak (0.208), yet this was under a single-profile, no-aggregation setup and with a fundamentally different encoder architecture, so it does not definitively rule out complementary image signal. 2) What this tests: config_030 pairs the best known RNA configuration (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) with the ResNet50 image branch via the simplest fusion (concat), isolating the question 'does adding the image modality to a strong RNA signal improve validation accuracy over RNA-only?' 3) Why it is the best use of budget: This is the highest-information experiment for the overall search. A positive result opens the entire multimodal design space (fusion strategy, image encoder, aggregation) and justifies further investment. A null or negative result eliminates ~30 multimodal configurations from consideration and redirects remaining budget toward RNA-encoder refinement (e.g., scgpt) or alternative image encoders (ViT-L). Testing this directional question before exploring encoder variants or fusion strategies avoids spending multiple experiments on a modality that may not contribute.

rows.experiment_summary: This experiment tested scgpt as the RNA encoder in the RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool setting, providing a clean single-variable comparison against both scvi_n200 (llm_summary_005, acc ~0.650) and PCA-2000 (llm_summary_003, acc ~0.591). The validation accuracy of ~0.530 (F1: ~0.515) indicates that scgpt underperformed scvi_n200 by approximately 0.12 and even the linear PCA-2000 baseline by ~0.06 in this controlled comparison, suggesting scvi_n200 remains the preferred learned RNA encoder and scgpt does not offer a competitive alternative in this configuration. It remains uncertain whether scgpt's underperformance reflects a limitation of its specific architecture or training regime on this dataset, whether it could behave differently under alternative aggregation strategies or in multimodal fusion settings, and whether other learned encoders (e.g., different latent dimensions or pretrained variants) might close the gap to scvi_n200.
rows.selection_reason: The current best configuration is RNA-only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool (config_005, acc 0.650). The RNA encoder is the dominant design choice since RNA is clearly the strongest modality (0.650 vs 0.208 for image-only), and all future multimodal experiments will build on the RNA backbone. However, scgpt—a second learned encoder—is completely untested, leaving a major gap in our understanding of the encoder landscape. Config_008 (RNA-only, multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_005, isolating the encoder effect while holding profile setting, aggregation, and modality fixed. This is the highest-information next experiment: if scgpt outperforms scvi_n200, it redefines the best RNA configuration and all subsequent multimodal experiments; if comparable, it confirms scvi_n200 as the preferred learned encoder; if worse, it rules out scgpt and narrows the search. Under a limited budget, resolving which RNA encoder is superior before further multimodal exploration is more informative than testing fusion variants or image encoders on a potentially suboptimal RNA backbone.

rows.experiment_summary: This experiment tested weighted fusion in place of concat fusion, holding all other variables identical to llm_summary_006 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, ResNet50), yielding a validation accuracy of ~0.678 (F1: ~0.646) compared to ~0.632 (F1: ~0.607) under concat. In this clean single-variable comparison, weighted fusion improved accuracy by approximately 0.046 and exceeded the RNA-only scvi_n200 baseline of ~0.650 (llm_summary_005), indicating that the ResNet50 image branch does carry complementary signal that was being diluted by unweighted concatenation. It remains uncertain whether stronger image encoders (e.g., ViT-L), alternative fusion mechanisms (e.g., gating or attention), or different weighting schemes could yield further gains beyond the current 0.678, and whether the residual improvement over the RNA-only baseline reflects meaningful multimodal headroom or is largely attributable to the weighted mechanism downweighting a still-weak image feature (0.208 alone).
rows.selection_reason: The current best configuration is config_005 (RNA-only, scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) at 0.650 accuracy. The only multimodal test (config_030: same RNA branch + ResNet50, concat fusion) yielded 0.632, a slight degradation. This raises the question of whether the underperformance is due to the naive concat fusion mechanism (which forces equal-weight combination of a strong RNA signal and a weak image signal) or due to the inherently weak ResNet50 image features (0.208 alone). Config_031 changes only the fusion strategy from concat to weighted, holding all other variables identical to config_030 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, ResNet50). This single-variable comparison cleanly isolates the fusion effect: if weighted fusion recovers or exceeds 0.650, it confirms that the image signal is useful but was being diluted by unweighted concatenation, validating the multimodal direction; if it does not help, it strongly implicates the ResNet50 encoder as the bottleneck, justifying a shift to ViT-L in subsequent experiments. This is the most informative next step because it resolves a critical design ambiguity with minimal confounding, directly informing whether further multimodal budget should be spent on better fusion or better image encoders.

rows.experiment_summary: This experiment tested ViT-L (imagenet_vit_l) as the image encoder in the multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool, weighted-fusion configuration, providing a clean single-variable comparison against the ResNet50 variant (llm_summary_008, acc ~0.678, F1 ~0.646). Validation accuracy improved to ~0.706 (F1: ~0.667), a gain of ~0.028 over ResNet50 and ~0.056 over the RNA-only scvi_n200 baseline (llm_summary_005, acc ~0.650), indicating in this controlled comparison that the stronger pretrained image encoder does unlock additional complementary signal beyond what ResNet50 contributed. It remains uncertain whether the observed gain reflects a fundamental ceiling on image information or is partly attributable to ViT-L's greater model capacity and pretraining scale, and whether alternative fusion mechanisms, different weighting schemes, or further encoder refinements could yield additional improvements on top of this new best configuration.
rows.selection_reason: The current best configuration (config_031: scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, ResNet50, weighted) achieves 0.678, exceeding the RNA-only baseline (0.650) by ~0.028, confirming the image branch carries complementary signal. However, ResNet50 alone yields only 0.208 accuracy, making it unclear whether the modest multimodal gain reflects a ceiling on image information or simply a weak encoder. Config_037 tests ViT-L as the image encoder while holding all other variables at their best-known settings (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion), providing a clean single-variable comparison against config_031. This directly addresses the highest-impact open question: can a stronger pretrained image encoder unlock substantially more complementary signal? A positive result would validate further investment in the multimodal branch and guide encoder/fusion refinement; a null result would indicate the image modality has limited headroom, redirecting budget toward RNA-side improvements (e.g., alternative aggregation with scvi_n200 via config_006). Under a limited budget, this experiment maximizes information gain about the most uncertain and potentially highest-leverage design axis.

rows.experiment_summary: This experiment tested transformer aggregation in place of avgpool, changing only the aggregation strategy while holding scvi_n200, ViT-L, multiprofile, and weighted fusion fixed relative to the prior best (llm_summary_009, acc ~0.706). In this clean single-variable comparison, transformer aggregation improved validation accuracy to ~0.725 (F1 ~0.685), a gain of ~0.019, reversing the prior finding under PCA-2000 where transformer underperformed avgpool by ~0.07 and suggesting that attention-based aggregation interacts favorably with the learned nonlinear 200-dim latent features of scvi_n200. It remains uncertain whether this modest gain is stable across runs, whether further transformer hyperparameter tuning could yield additional improvement, and whether other unexplored dimensions (e.g., alternative fusion mechanisms or encoder variants) could build on this new best configuration.
rows.selection_reason: The current best configuration (config_037: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted; acc 0.706) has only been tested with avgpool aggregation. The prior evidence from PCA-2000 (config_002 vs config_003) showed transformer underperforming avgpool by ~0.07, but that comparison used linear 2000-dim features; scvi_n200 produces learned, nonlinear 200-dim latent features that may interact differently with attention-based aggregation. Config_039 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding all other variables (scvi_n200, ViT-L, multiprofile, weighted fusion) fixed, providing a clean single-variable test of whether transformer aggregation can improve upon the current best. If it succeeds, it directly extends the best configuration; if it fails, it confirms avgpool is robustly optimal across encoder types and frees budget to explore other dimensions. This is the most efficient exploitation step given the strong evidence for the current configuration and the one remaining untested aggregation variant in the best-performing setup.
